result:
If I could keep one completely useless collection, it would be orphan keys.

Not valuable ones. Not gold or antique skeleton keys that belong in a museum. I mean the plain, scratched brass ones you find at the bottom of a junk drawer, mixed in with dead batteries and takeout menus. Keys whose locks have moved, or been changed, or been demolished entirely. Every house has at least two of them. Nobody throws them away, because throwing away a key feels strangely final — like admitting that whatever it opened is truly gone.

I love that hesitation.

Someone once held that key every single day. It lived warm in a pocket. It had a specific turn, a little wiggle to the left before it would catch. It opened a front door after a bad day at work, an apartment where someone learned to cook badly and then better, a locker, a diary, a first car that smelled like vinyl and old coffee. And now it does nothing at all, except wait in a drawer, just in case we remember.

I think about single gloves for the same reason.

Every winter, you start seeing them: one glove perched carefully on a fence post, or on top of a mailbox, or draped over a railing by a bus stop. Someone found it in the snow and instead of leaving it to get soaked and grey, they lifted it up and put it somewhere visible. It’s such a small, stubbornly optimistic act. The owner is probably never coming back. The glove will probably be there until spring. But for a minute, a stranger decided: *maybe.*

That might be my favorite kind of human behavior — the completely impractical caretaking of things that probably don’t matter anymore.

Refilling an empty ice tray for the next person. Straightening a crooked picture frame in a waiting room. Warning someone behind you in line that their backpack is open. Writing “You are here” on a map that’s already obvious. Leaving a perfect, untouched snowbank alone just because it looks nice.

None of it is efficient. None of it will be remembered. It just makes the world very slightly less lonely to move through.

I have a theory that a life isn’t really made of the big, labeled events we put in photo albums. It’s made of thresholds. The moment on the train platform between leaving and arriving. Standing in your kitchen at 11 p.m., refrigerator light on, not actually hungry, just thinking. The pause after you’ve parked the car but before you turn the engine off, finishing the last thirty seconds of a song. We spend so much time in-between, not quite who we were, not quite who we’re going to be yet.

Maybe that’s why we keep the orphan keys. Not because we think the door will come back.

Because we remember being the person who knew how to open it, and some part of us isn’t ready to set that down just yet.

And maybe that’s fine. Maybe we don’t have to make everything useful again. Some things can just be kept — a glove on a fence, a key in a drawer — as proof that once, it mattered, and someone noticed.
